verdict.reasoning: Patient reports symptoms started “five days ago,” has “quite dry” cough “maybe every 20, 30 minutes or so,” and nose is “just constantly streaming” and “constant streaming, like using a million tissues,” consistent with relentless rhinorrhea.
Same as cc-001: 5-day history, dry cough every 20–30 minutes, and constant nasal streaming are all explicitly described.

No SOB/chest pain/pleurisy/hemoptysis: Patient answers “No” to chest pain, “No, that’s all fine” to difficulty breathing or pain on deep breath, and “Nope” to coughing up blood. No history of chest infections: to “do you regularly have any infections in your chest” patient says “Normally, no.”
Patient states: “I’ve been feeling really hot… sometimes I’m feeling really chilly, needing to be under a blanket,” which supports intermittent fevers and chills even though temperature not measured.
Patient: “I’ve had quite achy muscles,” which is consistent with myalgias.

Patient: “around when it started. I had some diarrhea… But since then it’s all been pretty fine” and later answers “No” to “Vomiting, diarrhea now?” indicating only an early episode and no recent ongoing vomiting or diarrhea.
When asked “are you eating and drinking normally?” patient replies “Yes,” and doctor confirms “you’re drinking while holding down fluids,” supporting maintained appetite and fluid intake.

Doctor asks about passing water, frequency, and thirst: “Have you been able to pass water normally? Any increase in frequency… or any increased thirst?” Patient: “No, not particularly.” This supports no dysuria/polyuria/polydipsia. For weight: “has your weight been stable?” Patient: “Yeah.”
Rashes: Patient answers “No, nothing like that.” Headaches/vision: To “Headaches or change in your vision?” patient responds “No,” supporting absence of rashes, headaches, and vision changes.
Doctor: “with your diabetes, have you had a blood test recently?” Patient: “Yeah… it was normal. It was around three weeks ago.” This matches timing and reported normal result.
Early in consult patient says “normally I’m diabetic,” and later confirms medical problems are “just the hypertension and the diabetes.”
Patient: “I’ve got hypertension, so I’m on some drugs for that.” and repeats “just the hypertension and the diabetes.”
In response to “what type of drugs are you on?” patient says “something called metformin.”
Same answer: patient adds “and lisinopril, I think, is the other one.”

Patient: “Quite a few Lem Zips… Maybe two or three… at the start of the day and at the end of the day.” Doctor: “the lemcip I wouldn’t take. And that contains paracetamol, so don’t take any other paracetamol containing products with that.” This supports current use 2–3 times/day and that it contains paracetamol.
To “Do you have any allergies to anything?” patient: “I sometimes suffer from some, like hay fever.”
To “Any allergies to any medications at all?” patient: “Not that I’m aware of, no.” indicating no known drug allergies.
Doctor: “And do you smoke at all?” Patient: “No.”
Doctor: “Do you drink any alcohol?” Patient: “Yes, the odd sherry.” which corresponds to occasional sherry.
To “And do you work?” patient answers “Yes, I’m an office manager.”
Doctor: “Who do you live with at home?” Patient: “My partner and my dog.”
Doctor explicitly asks if patient has checked temperature; patient: “No, I haven’t.” No measurement is recorded during the visit, supporting that no temperature was measured.
Doctor: “What is your weight and height?” Patient: “My height is 5 foot 5 and my weight is 65 kg.”
Same quote: “My height is 5 foot 5 and my weight is 65 kg.”
Transcript contains no physical examination maneuvers or vital signs (no BP, HR, RR, SpO2, temp), so stating none were documented is accurate.

The doctor says “you probably have got an infection in the chest… most of the time these infections are caused by viruses,” but does not explicitly frame it as “acute upper respiratory tract infection versus viral bronchitis” or mention “low-grade” fever or “absence of red flags” as a formal differential; this diagnostic formulation is added.

While diabetes and hypertension are mentioned, control status is not stated as “well controlled”; doctor even asks if BP is unstable and patient “can’t remember,” so calling them well controlled goes beyond the transcript.

Doctor: “It’s fine to carry on what you’re doing at the moment with the lemcip… that contains paracetamol, so don’t take any other paracetamol containing products with that.” This supports supportive care and avoiding additional paracetamol.

Doctor: “it’s definitely worth getting a thermometer and checking your temperature” and later “if the temperature is ongoing above 37.5, 38, you keep spiking temperatures… then we certainly would need to speak to you again.”

Doctor advises: if temperature is “ongoing above 37.5, 38… and that’s not settling down… then we certainly would need to speak to you again,” which is red-flag advice regarding persistent/worsening fever.
Doctor: “if … your cough’s getting worse, you’re coughing up lots of nasty phlegm… then we certainly would need to speak to you again,” consistent with return if cough becomes productive/purulent.
Doctor: “or you cough up any blood… then we certainly would need to speak to you again,” which is hemoptysis.
Doctor: “or any shortness of breath… then we certainly would need to speak to you again.”
Doctor: “or your cough up… or get blood coming out your nose or any shortness of breath, chest pain, then we certainly would need to speak to you again,” including chest pain.
Same sentence: “or get blood coming out your nose… then we certainly would need to speak to you again,” advising return if nasal bleeding occurs.

Doctor, referencing diabetes and infection: “With the diabetes, you are a bit more likely to get a bacterial infection… so it’s something that we do need to be careful of.” And in response to patient asking about antibiotics: “Yeah, potentially. If it’s not settling or the temperature’s ongoing getting worse, then we definitely need to talk to you again,” implying antibiotics would be considered if bacterial features develop.
Doctor: “make sure that you have the regular diabetes and blood pressure checkups that your GP has asked you for,” which is maintaining routine monitoring.
